Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-03
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maeve Thompson (Redwood AE), Ibrahim Khan (Redwood SE), Sofia Li (Redwood Runtime Eng); Raj Patel (Polaris CTO), Elena Gomez (Polaris ML Infra Lead), Tom Brooks (Polaris SRE), Nina Alvarez (Polaris Infra Eng)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Deep dive into GPU runtime profiling comparing TensorRT-LLM and vLLM; kernel selection, CUDA graphs, KV cache behavior and batching tradeoffs discussed.
- Polaris to provide model and input distribution; Redwood to deliver perf spreadsheet and CUDA graph artifacts.
- Agree to run on-prem benchmarks in Polaris lab, scope quantization experiments and fallback policies for VPC/on-prem.

Topics: kernel selection, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM, CUDA graphs, KV cache/prefix caching, batching strategies, quantization impacts, VPC/on-prem constraints and benchmarking plan.

[00:00] Maeve Thompson: Alright, uh, thanks everyone for joining. We're gonna, uh, do a deep dive today on GPU runtime profiling  the TensorRT dash LLM vs vLLM comparison, kernel selection, and CUDA graphs. Ibrahim and Sofia from our runtime team will lead.

[00:18] Raj Patel: Thanks Maeve, appreciate it. We're mostly concerned with latency tail and cost per token on our internal chat assistant; we run 2k typical context, sometimes up to 8k. We also  our infra is partially on GCP GKE and we have an on-prem rack for sensitive data. So curious about on-prem behavior too.

[00:38] Ibrahim Khan: Cool. Quick agenda: 1) high-level primer on kernel selection and how it affects perf, 2) results and observations from initial TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM runs, 3) CUDA Graphs and warm-up behavior, 4) KV cache interactions and batching recommendations, 5) quantization caveats, 6) next steps for Polaris on-prem runs.

[00:55] Elena Gomez: Sounds good. Also we wanna understand when dedicated capacity or private (VPC/on-prem) makes sense vs just using hosted.

[01:05] Sofia Li: Yep, we'll try to call that out. Quick note  some of the terms may be slightly off in the transcript, I might say "Tren-RT" or "v-L-M" but it's TensorRT-LLM and vLLM.

[01:16] Ibrahim Khan: Right. So kernel selection  at a high level, the runtime picks kernels based on layer size, sequence length, and model architecture. For example, Triton/TensorRT kernels are often faster for dense transformer blocks if the input size aligns to their preferred tile sizes. vLLM's CUDA path uses fused kernels tuned for attention patterns we typically see in chat workloads; those can be better for variable-length streams.

[01:42] Tom Brooks: Can you give a concrete example? Like for a 3B model with 2k context, what's the delta look like?

[01:49] Ibrahim Khan: Sure  in our internal runs on A100 80GB, for a 3B llama-like model, TensorRT-LLM (with optimized kernels and FP16 INT8 profiles where applicable) showed ~1.6x throughput improvement at steady-state over vLLM when using large fixed batch sizes and long sequences. But vLLM tended to have ~20-30% lower 95th percentile latency for single-stream low-batch requests because it excels at minimizing kernel launch overhead via continuous batching.

[02:20] Raj Patel: So it's tradeoffs  TRT for throughput, vLLM for tail latency. Is that always the case?

[02:25] Sofia Li: Not always. TRT's advantage depends on kernel coverage and whether TF32/FP16 paths are fully supported for every op. There's also compilation time and kernel fallback behavior  if a kernel isn't available, TRT falls back to a reference path which kills perf. vLLM's CPU-GPU scheduling and micro-batching logic can beat TRT in mixed workloads.

[02:43] Nina Alvarez: What about CUDA Graphs? We're seeing big warm-up times for cold starts in our on-prem cluster.

[02:50] Ibrahim Khan: Great question. CUDA Graphs can dramatically reduce kernel launch overhead for repeated execution graphs  especially beneficial for stable sequence length and fixed batch shapes. For example, capturing a CUDA Graph for an autoregressive step where shapes are stable can reduce launch overhead by 30-60% depending on the model size and token generation pattern. But they require deterministic shapes and careful handling of KV cache pointer updates.

[03:14] Elena Gomez: Is there complexity with dynamic sequence lengths? Our workloads vary a lot.

[03:20] Ibrahim Khan: Yes  dynamic lengths complicate graph reuse. Two approaches: 1) use a small set of pre-captured graphs for common shapes (e.g., 1, 8, 32 tokens) and fall back to a non-graph path for rare shapes; 2) use runtime shape normalization/padding so inputs map to one of the captured graphs. Each has tradeoffs: padding increases compute and memory; fallback adds latency unpredictability.

[03:44] Raj Patel: Any gotchas for KV cache? We use long chats with repeated context and we rely on prefix caching a lot.

[03:51] Sofia Li: KV cache memory layout and eviction policy are crucial. TRT implementations often prefer contiguous KV layouts optimized for their kernels, whereas vLLM focuses on sparse append-friendly layouts for streaming. If your workload reuses prefixes heavily, a contiguous layout plus batched KV reads is best. But if you stream many small contexts concurrently, vLLM style appendable caches reduce copy overhead.

[04:16] Tom Brooks: So in practice, if we have mixed streams  some long single-user chats and many short assistant calls  what do you recommend?

[04:24] Ibrahim Khan: We usually recommend a hybrid routing policy: route latency-sensitive single-user chats to a vLLM-optimized pool (lower tail), route high-throughput batch requests or long-context offline generation to TensorRT-optimized instances. Redwood's smart routing can do that automatically based on SLO tags.

[04:45] Raj Patel: That sounds promising. How does quantization affect kernel selection? We were hoping to use INT8 for cost savings.

[04:52] Sofia Li: INT8 quant is great for throughput and cost but has model-dependent quality regressions. TensorRT's INT8 kernels are very fast but require calibration or per-channel scaling; not all ops get INT8 kernels, leading to mixed-precision paths. vLLM has FP16 + quantization-aware runtimes in the community, but less mature INT8 kernel coverage. Important to run output-quality evals against your prompts  Redwood's Optimize tool can suggest quant profiles and run regressions.

[05:25] Elena Gomez: About on-prem deployment: we run inside a VPC with strict egress policies. Any networking or KMS gotchas?

[05:33] Maeve Thompson: For Private VPC/on-prem, Redwood supports an air-gapped option and customer-managed KMS. The main operational differences are: 1) you manage driver / CUDA versions and we provide recommended images, 2) we need to coordinate kernel/driver combos for TensorRT versions, and 3) for CUDA Graphs you need consistent driver levels across nodes to avoid subtle ABI mismatches.

[05:55] Nina Alvarez: Which driver+CUDA+TensorRT combos are recommended?

[05:59] Ibrahim Khan: We typically recommend CUDA 12.x with matching drivers and TensorRT 8.x for best TensorRT-LLM support on Ampere+ GPUs. We provide a compatibility matrix; we'll send that matrix as part of the follow-up.

[06:11] Tom Brooks: About profiling: what traces should we collect to make your profiling useful?

[06:16] Ibrahim Khan: Good question. Ideal traces: 1) per-request latency timeline with timestamps (server receive, enqueue, kernel launches, token emitted), 2) CUDA kernel traces (Nsight or CUPTI) for a representative 1-2 minute workload, 3) memory usage / KV cache stats, 4) model config and tokenizer + input distribution, 5) quantization profiles if you've tried them. We can ingest the traces and produce annotated call-outs about kernel hotspots.

[06:42] Raj Patel: Ok. Can you walk us through one of your profiling runs  maybe a TensorRT-LLM run that shows kernel selection differences?

[06:49] Ibrahim Khan: Sure. Example: 7B model, 2k context, batch size 1 streaming. On A100, we saw that initially the TRT runtime selected large GEMM kernels for attention and a fused MLP kernel. Kernel timelines showed long GEMM durations but fewer launches. vLLM's run used more smaller fused attention kernels which increased kernel launch counts but each was shorter. By capturing a CUDA Graph around the attention+mlp sequence we replaced thousands of launches with a single graph invocation per token which cut overhead. But for variable token lengths the graph hit rate dropped so benefits reduced.

[07:28] Elena Gomez: Any examples of kernel fallbacks that caused perf surprises?

[07:32] Ibrahim Khan: Yes  one customer had TensorRT fall back to device function implementations for a custom RoPE variant; that fallback path used non-optimized kernels and latencies spiked 3x for certain layers. We recommend running a small test to see if TRT reports any fallbacks; the logs usually mention missing kernel implementations.

[07:54] Maeve Thompson: Quick interjection  Raj, did you say you're using a RoPE-attention variant?

[07:59] Raj Patel: We use a rotary encoding similar to RoPE; it's in our fork of the model.

[08:03] Ibrahim Khan: Then we should check kernel coverage for that encoding. If it's not supported by TRT kernels, possible mitigations: 1) add a small wrapper to convert to supported ops, 2) keep that path on vLLM or a TPU-like kernel, or 3) accept a mixed path with perf impact.

[08:21] Tom Brooks: About memory  does kv cache layout choice affect memory fragmentation across nodes?

[08:28] Sofia Li: Yes, fragmentation can be an issue. Contiguous allocation strategies are simpler but can lead to wasted reserved memory if you over-provision for max context. A good pattern: allocate per-stream pools sized to common context percentiles and have a fallback allocation for rare long contexts. That reduces page faults and memory churn.

[08:49] Raj Patel: Can you explain continuous batching vs micro-batching  our SREs are confused about how to configure that.

[08:56] Ibrahim Khan: Continuous batching (vLLM-style) aggregates incoming requests opportunistically and launches larger kernels when available; it's great for lowering latency when arrival rates are moderate because you don't wait for a full batch. Micro-batching (TensorRT setups) uses small, fixed batch sizes to keep kernel shapes stable and enable CUDA Graph capture. The config levers are: max_batch_latency, max_batch_size, and prefer_latency vs prefer_throughput modes.

[09:21] Elena Gomez: For our SLA, 95th < 250ms for single conversations is important. Which setup likely meets that?

[09:28] Ibrahim Khan: vLLM pools tuned for low max_batch_latency (e.g., 3-5ms) and small max_batch_size often meet strict tail SLOs for single-conversation workloads. If you're generating many tokens per response, dedicated instances with optimized kernels can help too, but you may need to use smart routing to avoid hiccups.

[09:46] Nina Alvarez: Any notes on telemetry overhead? We're worried traces will add too much noise.

[09:52] Sofia Li: Keep perf counters lightweight in prod: sample kernel traces for short windows, use metrics aggregation for long-term trends. CUPTI full tracing is heavy  do it on a staging run. Also, for on-prem, ensure you have permissions for device tracing tools.

[10:08] Raj Patel: Let's talk quantization strategy: per-channel vs per-tensor, calibration data size, and fallback thresholds.

[10:14] Ibrahim Khan: Per-channel quantization is typically better for transformer weights  it preserves dynamic range per output channel. Calibration dataset should mirror your prompt distribution, especially rare tokens/context. Fallback thresholds: run A/B with a small eval set and set automatic rollback for prompts where logprob changes exceed a delta. Redwood Optimize can automate some of this.

[10:36] Tom Brooks: Do you have any public scripts or examples for running these bench traces?

[10:41] Maeve Thompson: Yes  we'll share a benchmark repo and a small harness that runs mixed arrival patterns, captures CUPTI traces, and collects per-token latencies. Maeve: action to send link.

[10:50] Raj Patel: From a cost perspective, any rough numbers for INT8 vs FP16 vs FP32?

[10:56] Sofia Li: Rough rule of thumb: INT8 can double throughput vs FP16 on supported kernels; FP16 is typically 1.5-2x vs FP32. The real delta depends on kernel coverage and memory bandwidth. Also consider inference density  you get more QPS per GPU which lowers unit cost, but the upfront engineering for calibration and checks matters.

[11:18] Elena Gomez: About on-prem scheduling: we use Slurm historically for batch  not Kubernetes. Any compatibility issues?

[11:25] Ibrahim Khan: Redwood Private supports container images you can run under Slurm, but you need to expose NVIDIA container runtime and ensure driver matching. We have runbooks for Slurm and Nomad; for the Trt-LLM profiling we recommend a small Kubernetes-like wrapper or at least consistent container runtime flags.

[11:42] Nina Alvarez: Does Redwood support mixed GPU fleets  like A100 + L40s?

[11:48] Sofia Li: Yes, but kernel selection and performance profiles differ by GPU. We recommend grouping similar GPU types into pools and routing requests by model profile; mixing in the same pool complicates kernel selection and can cause unpredictable perf.

[11:59] Raj Patel: Are there specific ops that cause TRT to not have kernels?

[12:03] Ibrahim Khan: Custom attention variants, exotic activation functions, and some rotary/rope variants. Also certain fused MLP patterns if the model uses non-standard bias patterns. The TRT logs show missing plugin messages; that's the fastest way to detect.

[12:19] Tom Brooks: Any tips for reducing cold-start latency besides CUDA Graphs?

[12:24] Ibrahim Khan: Prefill the KV cache for frequent prefixes, keep a small warm pool of pre-initialized contexts, and use faster cold-start paths (smaller models for bootstrapping). Also warm-up kernels with a synthetic trace at deploy time.

[12:38] Elena Gomez: For our on-prem benchmark, we'd like you to run both TRT and vLLM paths and show per-kernel timelines. Can you do that in our environment?

[12:45] Maeve Thompson: Yes, we can do joint runs. We'll need SSH and lab access for a short window and a contact on your side.

[12:52] Raj Patel: We'll arrange that. Who should we give access to?

[12:55] Maeve Thompson: IAM for Ibrahim and Sofia; Maia will also coordinate but main contacts are Ibrahim and Sofia. We'll also need a sample model checkpoint and a set of representative prompts.

[13:06] Ibrahim Khan: We'll prepare a profiling checklist. Quick note on kernels: sometimes you can influence kernel selection by adjusting layer order in the serialized engine or by enabling certain TensorRT plugins. We'll document the knobs.

[13:18] Nina Alvarez: Any security notes for on-prem profiling? We can't send model weights off-site.

[13:23] Maeve Thompson: Understood. We can run profiling entirely on your infrastructure with Redwood Private installed; we can also accept traces instead of weights. If you prefer, we'll give a runbook you can execute and then send the traces.

[13:34] Raj Patel: Ok good. What about fallback policies if the TRT path fails in production?

[13:40] Sofia Li: We recommend a layered fallback: try TensorRT-LLM optimized pool, if kernel fallback or OOM detected, automatically route to vLLM pool with preserved KV cache semantics where possible. Redwood runtime can do transparent fallbacks and metrics tagging so you can see when fallbacks happen.

[13:58] Tom Brooks: Does fallback preserve response determinism?

[14:02] Ibrahim Khan: Not necessarily  different kernels and precisions can slightly change outputs. We tag responses to indicate which pool produced them so you can do quality monitoring and set auto-rollbacks.

[14:15] Raj Patel: On the practical side, how long do you think the on-prem benchmark will take?

[14:21] Ibrahim Khan: For a full run (TensorRT + vLLM + quantization profiles + kernel traces) plan for 1-2 days of run time including setup and data collection. The actual computational trace capture window might be a few hours.

[14:34] Maeve Thompson: Great. Quick recap before we close: 1) Redwood to send benchmark repo, compatibility matrix, and initial perf spreadsheet. 2) Polaris to provide model checkpoint, tokenizer and input distribution. 3) Schedule on-prem benchmarking window (week of 2026-03-16). 4) Ibrahim to prepare CUDA Graph capture examples and kernel selection notes.

[14:58] Raj Patel: Sounds good. Anything else?

[15:01] Elena Gomez: One more question  how do you measure perceptual quality after quantization? We wanna avoid regressions for our main customer flows.

[15:08] Sofia Li: Use a prompt-based eval set representing critical flows; measure generation divergence using logprob deltas, embedding similarity, and human-in-the-loop checks for top N prompts. Redwood's Optimize can automate this and tie alerts to rolling quantization.

[15:25] Tom Brooks: Ok I think that's it from us. We'll get the artifacts to you.

[15:29] Maeve Thompson: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and next steps.

[15:34] Raj Patel: Thanks all.
